items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: He was a classical musician that could play jazz also and had recorded some duets with the famous Stephane Grappelly in France.

ctx.x: In December 1940, Barney Josephson branched out and opened a Cafe Society Uptown on East 58th Street, and it was a real plushy joint. The Cafe Society Downtown was not a very large place, and there was only one small dressing room for musicians and entertainers. But at the Uptown, the whole building was occupied by the club and there was a big dressing room for the two bands, the Golden Gate Quartet and the Boogie Woogies. There were at least 4 other dressing rooms quite large and they were all on the third floor.

The club featured Teddy Wilson and Eddie South's orchestra, the Gates, the Boogies without Joe Turner, Hazel Scott and a comedian named Penner. Eddie South was a violinist known as "the Dark Angel" of that instrument and had been trained by some of the finest violin professors in Europe and especially in Hungaria. He was a classical musician that could play jazz also and had recorded some duets with the famous Stephane Grappelly in France.

Eddie had the bassist Dole Dickens, a fine classical and jazz pianist named Stanley Facey and the well known drummer Gordon "Specs" Powell to accompany him. Eddie was one of the attractions in the floor show and also played for dancing when we had our intermissions.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: The 12th of November I recorded under my own name with Stephane Grappelli... Grappelli surprised me by playing piano on some of the numbers.

ctx.x: It was a strange formation to me because it consisted of three guitars, a violin and bass violin. I had never heard any groups like them for the simple reason that none like them had ever existed. The violin player was the best I had ever heard playing jazz after Robert "Juice" Wilson on one, the guitarist was the greatest I had ever heard because guitars in those days, most guitar players played rhythm style. But this fellow took solos and had ideas and techniques that were out of this world.

The violinist spoke English and told me that his name was Stephane Grappelli. The solo guitarist was Django Reinhardt and the other guitarist was Django's brother Joseph. The bass was Louis Vola and Pierre Ferret who played rhythm guitar with Joseph.

Grappelli told me that Django and Joseph were gypsies. Django had had an accident with his left hand when he was younger and could only use three fingers. But he used those three fingers as if they were ten.
